title: Experiments on Society
description: A mouse utopia that collapsed, the Hawthorne effect rechecked, and letters dropped on purpose

concepts.title: Universe 25: A Paradise for Mice
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1968 John B. Calhoun, a researcher at the National Institute of Mental Health, put four pairs of mice into a pen designed as a paradise. Food and water never ran out and nesting material was plentiful. The only thing in short supply was space.1 The pen, called Universe 25, was a tank 101 inches (2.6 m) square with no predators, a steady temperature and 256 nest boxes, each big enough for fifteen mice.2

At first the population doubled about every 55 days. After day 315 growth slowed, and mouse society came apart. Males gave up defending territory, nursing mothers attacked their own young, and a group Calhoun called "the beautiful ones" did nothing but eat, sleep and groom, never fighting and never mating. On day 560 the population peaked at 2,200, far below what the boxes could hold. After about day 600 almost no young survived, and even when numbers fell back to early levels there was no recovery.3 Calhoun reported the collapse in 1973 under the title "Death Squared."4

He had coined a name for this kind of breakdown in a 1962 Scientific American article about crowded rats: the behavioral sink. The phrase escaped the lab. Tom Wolfe used it to describe rush-hour New York, and Calhoun's rodents were soon taken as "scientific evidence" that crowded inner cities bred social decay. Calhoun invited the comparison by calling some of his animals "juvenile delinquents" and "social dropouts." Yet studies of people found no consistent link between density and pathology, and some found the reverse. His own message was also more hopeful than the legend: he tried to design spaces that would help crowded rodents cope. The historians Edmund Ramsden and Jon Adams argue that a simplified, popular version of his work came to overshadow that more nuanced message.5

concepts.title: The Hawthorne Effect, Rechecked
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1924 the National Research Council began an experiment at Western Electric's Hawthorne plant in Cicero, Illinois, which employed roughly 35,000 people. The question was narrow: does better lighting make workers more productive? Over eight years it grew into some of the most influential studies in social science, and the textbook version of its first result is startling. Every change in the lights, even dimming them, seemed to raise output.1

The archives at Harvard Business School tell a plainer story. The lighting tests ran from 1924 to 1927 in three departments, and accounts of them found no significant link between light and output. From 1927 the researchers moved five women who assembled telephone relays into a separate test room and varied their rest breaks and working hours. Output rose, but nobody could say whether the cause was the breaks, the shorter hours, wage incentives, the small group or the special attention the women received.2 The idea that people in a study change their behavior because they know they are being observed became known as the Hawthorne effect.3

For decades the lighting data were thought to be destroyed. Then the economists Steven Levitt and John List tracked them down and analyzed them for the first time. Their verdict, published in 2011, was that the famous descriptions of remarkable patterns in the data were "entirely fictional."4 The records had survived in a microfiche room in a small Milwaukee library and a forgotten archive in Boston. Output did rise on Mondays when the lights were changed, but it rose just as much on Mondays when nothing changed, and dips that seemed to follow the end of an experiment were ordinary summer slowdowns. The only signs of a real effect were faint, such as slightly higher output while experiments were running.5

concepts.title: Letters Dropped on Purpose
concepts.contentHtml:
Picture a sealed, stamped envelope lying on a sidewalk. Most people who find one will drop it in a mailbox. After his famous obedience experiments at Yale, the psychologist Stanley Milgram saw that this small courtesy could be turned into a measuring instrument. He and his colleagues "lost" letters on sidewalks and in stores around New Haven, Connecticut, and counted how many came back.1

The trick was in the addresses. The stamped letters were identical except for the recipient: "Medical Research Associates," a private individual, "Friends of the Communist Party" or "Friends of the Nazi Party." More than 70% of the letters to the medical group and to the private person were mailed, but only about 25% of those to the Communist and Nazi groups.2 In Cold War America, posting or binning a stranger's letter was a vote nobody knew they had cast.

The method's strength is that nobody knows they are in a study. A survey records what people say; a lost letter records what they do when no one is watching, which makes it an unobtrusive way to measure attitudes.3 Milgram, by then at Harvard, used it in 1964 to predict the outcome of the Johnson-Goldwater presidential race.4 Researchers still drop letters. In 2012 a team scattered them across 20 London neighborhoods and found that letters dropped in the poorest areas had 91% lower odds of being returned than those in the wealthiest.5 The finders are whoever happens to walk by, so a lost letter measures a place more than a person.

title: Rumors That Ran
description: Poisoned Halloween candy, the rumor of Orléans, and the great toilet paper panic of 1973

concepts.title: The Poisoned Candy That Wasn't
concepts.contentHtml:
Every October, parents are told to check trick-or-treat bags for razor blades and poison. The sociologist Joel Best decided to count the cases. With a student he searched four newspapers from 1958 to 1984 for reports of contaminated treats, and he has updated the tally every year since. Most reports described a treat that was found, not a child who was hurt, and many proved to be hoaxes. Best has been unable to find a single substantiated case of a child killed or seriously injured by a contaminated treat picked up while trick-or-treating.1

The deaths blamed on "Halloween sadism" fell apart on inspection. A five-year-old in Detroit who died in 1970 was said to have eaten heroin hidden in his candy; a less publicized follow-up reported that he had found the drug in a relative's home. Other deaths turned out to be natural or caused by illness.2 One child really was poisoned. On Halloween 1974 in Pasadena, Texas, eight-year-old Timothy O'Bryan ate a Pixy Stix laced with cyanide and died that night. It came from his father, Ronald, who had recently increased the life insurance on his children. To cover his tracks he handed poisoned sticks to four other children, and later claimed the candy came from a house on their trick-or-treat route.3 He was convicted of murdering his son and executed in 1984.4

Why does the fear survive? Best treats Halloween sadism as a contemporary legend: a story told as true even though there is little or no evidence it happened, which gives people a way to voice a wider fear that they are no longer safe. Warnings swell after real crimes. After deaths from poisoned Tylenol capsules in September 1982, newspaper reports of tampered treats jumped to 12 that year, from none the year before. Meanwhile the real danger of Halloween is traffic: children are four times as likely to be struck by a car on Halloween as on other nights.5

concepts.title: The Rumor of Orléans
concepts.contentHtml:
In May 1969 a story ran through Orléans, in central France. Young women shopping in certain downtown clothing boutiques were said to be drugged, then carried through secret tunnels to the Loire, where boats waited to take them abroad into forced prostitution. Some versions added a submarine.1 Every shop the story accused was run by a Jewish merchant, and none of it was true: no woman had gone missing. It was an antisemitic rumor, and for nearly two months, during a presidential campaign, it gripped the city.2

The rumor grew as it traveled. Henri Licht, one of the accused shopkeepers, found the story so absurd that at first he ignored it. Then, he recalled, it was no longer one woman but three, then seven, then fifteen, then thirty-eight. On 30 May a hostile crowd of several hundred gathered outside his shop, pointing and hurling insults. Eliane Klein, a teacher whose family ran one of the shops, alerted journalists and anti-racism groups, and the national press took up the affair.3

That summer the sociologist Edgar Morin came to Orléans with a team of his Paris students. The fitting-room abduction tale, they found, was not new: it had circulated for years in many French towns, Paris included, without any mention of Jews. But once it took root in a provincial city, Morin argued, an "irresistible force" fixed it on the Jewish shopkeeper, the old scapegoat for anxiety and guilt. It spread fastest among teenage girls and their parents, for whom the new boutiques stood for miniskirts and modern freedoms that felt like a threat.4 By the time the team arrived the rumor was already dead, finished off by its own excess and by the people who fought it. A case Morin learned of later showed what happens when nobody fights back: three years earlier the same story had targeted a shopkeeper and her two daughters in Rouen. They were not Jewish, no one came to their defense, and they were forced to leave the city.5

concepts.title: The Toilet Paper Panic of 1973
concepts.contentHtml:
By late 1973 Americans had learned to expect shortages. An Arab oil embargo had sent fuel prices soaring, and gasoline, electricity and even onions were reported to be scarce. Then Harold Froehlich, a Republican congressman from Wisconsin, found that the federal government's purchasing agency had fallen far short of the bids it needed to supply its own toilet paper. On December 11 he issued a press release warning that "the U.S. may face a serious shortage of toilet paper within a few months."1

Wire services and broadcasters ran with the story, and the word "may" tended to get lost. Then Johnny Carson joked about it on The Tonight Show in front of some 20 million viewers: "I'm not kidding. I saw it in the papers. There's a shortage of toilet paper!" He later apologized on air and told viewers there was no shortage, but by then it was too late.2 Shoppers rushed to grab as many rolls as they could. Manufacturers said nothing was limiting their output, yet stores could not keep up, and every bare shelf seemed to prove the rumor true. The frenzy lasted for months.3

Sociologists call this a self-fulfilling prophecy, a phrase coined by Robert K. Merton: a false belief leads people to act in ways that make it come true.4 There was no shortage until people believed in one, and then the rush to beat the shortage created it. Toilet paper is unusually exposed to this. In spring 2020 every US toilet paper mill was running, yet on one April day nearly half of American grocery stores ran out for at least part of the day. Stores keep only a few weeks' worth in their warehouses, so a burst of panic buying empties them long before factories can catch up.5

title: Gifts, Feasts and Status
description: Shell treasures you must give away, the potlatch and its ban, and Veblen's showy spending

concepts.title: The Kula Ring: Treasures You Must Give Away
concepts.contentHtml:
After six years in the South Seas and Australia, the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski went sightseeing in Edinburgh Castle and was shown the Crown jewels. As the keeper told their stories, Malinowski found them ugly and useless, and was reminded of the worn shell valuables of the Trobriand Islands, off New Guinea, whose holders named them and recited their histories with reverence. In both cases, he decided, the value came from owning them and the renown that went with it.1

The Trobriand valuables traveled in the kula, which he described in Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922). Communities on a wide ring of islands passed two kinds of object, and only two, in opposite directions: long necklaces of red shell, soulava, moved clockwise, and armshells of white shell, mwali, moved counterclockwise. Each was swapped for one of the other kind coming the other way, between partners for life, some living hundreds of miles apart.2

The odd rule is that nobody keeps them. A man in the kula holds a piece for a year or two at most, and even that can earn him a name for being slow and mean.3 The best pieces have their own names and histories, so holding one is like having a famous heirloom pass briefly through your hands. Trobrianders kept the kula apart from ordinary haggling barter, gimwali, and one insult for a clumsy partner was that he conducted his kula as if it were gimwali.4 The exchange outlived its famous visitor. Decades later, the anthropologist Annette Weiner reported that a few men still made armshells for kula exchanges, and that a kula man's shells and partners passed to a son or a sister's son.5

concepts.title: The Potlatch: Rich Is Who Gives Most
concepts.contentHtml:
The Kwakwaka'wakw of the British Columbia coast, as their U'mista Cultural Society explains, see a rich and powerful person not as someone who has a lot but as someone who gives the most away. The word potlatch, from the Chinook trade jargon, means "to give". A potlatch marks the great moments of life: naming a child, a marriage, passing on rights and privileges, mourning the dead. The guests are witnesses, they receive gifts, and the more that is given, the higher the status the host achieves.1

Officials and missionaries saw the potlatch as a barrier to assimilation, and its giving clashed with the settler ideal of piling up wealth. An amendment to the Indian Act dated 19 April 1884, in force from 1 January 1885, made taking part a crime. The ban lasted until 1951 and is recognized today as part of cultural genocide.2

On Christmas Day 1921, Chief Dan Cranmer hosted a potlatch at 'Mimkwamlis on Village Island, with at least 300 guests. Officials charged 45 people and offered a bargain: no jail if the community gave up potlatching and surrendered its masks, costumes and headdresses. Most agreed, yet 20 men and women still went to prison for two or three months, and, by the Canadian Museum for Human Rights' count, 750 potlatch items were taken.3 The Indian agent put them on show in the Alert Bay parish hall, charging admission, and sold 33 pieces to a New York collector; most of the rest were shipped to museums in Ottawa and Toronto.4

The law was never formally repealed. When the Indian Act was revised in 1951 the section was simply deleted, and the Kwakwaka'wakw had hoped for a stronger statement. In earlier days, a captive who made it home was said to have u'mista, and the return of the treasures is a form of u'mista too. Most of the Potlatch Collection is now home, at the U'mista Cultural Centre in Alert Bay and the Nuyumbalees Cultural Centre at Cape Mudge.5

concepts.title: Conspicuous Consumption: The Price Is the Point
concepts.contentHtml:
Put two spoons side by side. One is hand-wrought silver, worth ten to twenty dollars; the other is machine-made aluminum, worth ten to twenty cents. In 1899 the economist Thorstein Veblen pointed out that the costly spoon does its job no better, and argued that much of what we admire as its beauty is really our sense of its cost.1

His book was The Theory of the Leisure Class, and its argument was that wealth wins respect only when other people can see it. So the rich put it on display through conspicuous leisure, visibly not working, and conspicuous consumption, visibly spending, including on presents and feasts that turn guests into witnesses. Veblen named "the potlatch or the ball" as costly entertainments of exactly this kind.2 That was an outsider's reading of a ceremony with far more to it, as the previous story shows.

In 1950 the economist Harvey Leibenstein gave one part of the idea a name. The Veblen effect, he wrote, is the extent to which demand for a good rises because it bears a higher rather than a lower price. He kept it separate from the snob effect, in which demand falls as more other people buy the same thing.3

Researchers still test the idea. In a 2007 study, the economists Kerwin Kofi Charles, Erik Hurst and Nikolai Roussanov reasoned that if visible goods are status signals, they should matter most where the people you are compared with are poorer. Using US spending data and state incomes, they found that spending on visible goods such as clothing, jewelry and cars did fall as the average income of a household's reference group rose, separately within each racial group, and that differences in reference-group income explained most of the racial gaps in visible spending.4

title: Strange Towns
description: Muncie as "typical" Middletown, Ford's Amazon town, and Longyearbyen's rule against coffins

concepts.title: Middletown: The Search for a Typical Town
concepts.contentHtml:
In the 1920s, Robert and Helen Lynd led a research team into a small Indiana city to study all of its life: earning a living, making a home, raising children, leisure, religion and civic life. Their 1929 book called the city Middletown; it was Muncie.1 One resident told them they could save themselves the trouble: "I can tell you what's happening in just four letters: a-u-t-o!" Families seemed to put the car ahead of almost anything. Of 26 car-owning families whose bathrooms the interviewers happened to ask about, 21 lived in homes without bathtubs, though the Lynds warned that this little sample did not hold for car owners in general.2

Choosing the city meant deciding what "typical" should mean. The Lynds wanted a place as representative as possible of American life, yet small and uniform enough to study whole: a Midwestern city of 25,000 to 50,000 with a small Black and foreign-born population, so they could study cultural change without also studying racial change. Such a homogeneous, native-born population, they admitted, was unusual in an American industrial city, and the study mostly confined itself to white residents. They were candid about it: "A typical city, strictly speaking, does not exist."3

The label stuck anyway. The Lynds returned in the 1930s to see what the Depression had done, marketers flocked to Muncie to test new products, and in the late 1970s sociologists led by Theodore Caplow repeated the study fifty years on.4 In 1999 Caplow's team came back for Middletown IV, using the same survey questions in the same place with the same wording as the Lynds seventy-five years earlier.5 That is Middletown's real value: not that Muncie is America in miniature, but that one city has been measured the same way again and again for most of a century.

concepts.title: Fordlandia: Main Street in the Amazon
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1927 Henry Ford's company took a concession of 2.5 million acres beside the Tapajós River in the Brazilian Amazon to grow its own rubber, and planned far more than a plantation: a Midwestern town with Cape Cod-style houses, schools and health care, whole-wheat bread and unpolished rice, poetry recitations and square dances on weekends. Ford himself never once visited Brazil.1

Life ran on Dearborn's rules. Managers campaigned against liquor and the brothels that served a mostly single, male workforce, and unmarried workers had to eat in the company dining hall, where the menu ran to oatmeal and canned peaches from Michigan. When the hall replaced its waiters with a cafeteria line, the workers rebelled. On 22 December 1930 they smashed the dining hall, the time clocks and much of the settlement, while the American managers escaped by boat. No one was killed.2 The deeper clash was over time itself. A whistle on the water tower, audible seven miles away, called shifts and meals. "Before the coming of Ford," wrote the historian Greg Grandin, "Tapajós workers lived time, they didn't measure it."3

Nature won the longer war: planted close together in neat rows, the rubber trees were ravaged by leaf blight and insects. In 1939 the plantation workers even unionized, years before Ford's own River Rouge plant in Michigan signed a union contract.4 The company moved its main effort downriver to a second town, Belterra, but in 1945 Henry Ford II handed the plantations to the Brazilian government for $244,200, after a 20-year venture that had cost about $20 million.5

concepts.title: Longyearbyen and the Ban on Dying That Isn't
concepts.contentHtml:
For years a rumor has claimed that dying is illegal in Longyearbyen, the main town of Svalbard, Norway's Arctic archipelago. It is nonsense, but it grew from something real. The town's old cemetery took coffin burials from 1918 to 1950, including seven victims of the 1918 flu, buried in a separate row. After that the dead were taken to the mainland, because bodies are preserved in the permafrost and for fear that a pathogen might return.1 A 2008 regulation spells out today's rule: a grave in Longyearbyen means an urn grave, coffin graves are not allowed, and anyone who lived on Svalbard at the time of death has the right to one.2

The flu graves were once put to the test. In August 1998 researchers opened them, hoping to recover the 1918 virus, and took 50 samples of lung tissue and windpipe. But the coffins had been found above the permafrost rather than in it, which the project's Norwegian coordinator admitted made the puzzle harder.3

The deeper reason so few people die in Longyearbyen is that so few grow old there. It is a place people come to work, not somewhere they can spend their entire lives, and the average stay is about seven years.4 As a rule, births happen on the mainland too. Of the 2,504 people living in Longyearbyen and Ny-Ålesund in the second half of 2026, just 53 were 67 or older, while more than four in five were aged 20 to 66.5 The result is a sociological oddity: a town where people are rarely born and rarely grow old, because they come to work and then leave.
